m8.q: “A test that passes and nobody sees doesn't exist.” What fixes that?
o: A published report with evidence + requirement→test→execution traceability in the test management tool
A Slack notification when it passes
Leaving the logs in the CI console
m8.why: Visibility = a published report with evidence + a traceability chain anyone can audit.

m8.q: You change companies: they use TestRail instead of Xray. What changes in your method?
o: Everything: you have to relearn it
Nothing fundamental: the requirement→case→execution→evidence chain is the same; only the tool changes
m8.why: The standard is the concept, not the brand. That's why the method is tool-agnostic.

m8.q: What makes a green in the report defensible?
o: Attached evidence (steps, screenshot/response) you can explain if you're audited
m8.why: “The report is what you sign”: every green without explainable evidence is a bounced check.

m8.q: When do you capture screenshots/attachments in the suite?
o: Always, on every step of every test
Automatically on every FAILURE + at the key evidence steps — a balance between size and probative value
m8.why: A failure without evidence forces a re-run to “see what happened”; capturing everything all the time makes the report unmanageable. The criterion is probative value.

m8.q: The report says “512 passed, 3 failed” and nothing else. What does it need to be a report of the method?
o: Per-case detail: steps, evidence, failure category and which requirement each test covers
m8.why: A counter is not evidence. Without per-case detail you can't audit, classify or certify anything about those 512 greens.

o: That the report comes in two formats
From a requirement I reach its tests and their status; from any test I reach the requirement it covers
That it syncs twice a day
m8.why: The two directions answer different questions: “what covers this user story?” and “why does this test exist?”. Both must have an answer.

m8.q: A failure can be: a product bug, a broken test, or an environment/data problem. Why classify them in the report?
o: Because each category triggers a different action (report / fix the suite / fix the environment) and mixed metrics lie
m8.why: If 40% of your reds are environment, your suite isn't “bad”: your environment is. Without classification that signal doesn't exist and trust is lost.

m8.q: What does the execution HISTORY give you that a single run doesn't?
o: Trends: tests that became flaky, modules that degrade, growing duration — the movie, not the snapshot
Nothing, it just takes up disk
m8.why: A test that failed once is noise; one that fails in 20% of runs is a pattern. Only the history tells them apart.

m8.q: What do you attach to an API failure so the dev can pick it up without asking you anything else?
o: The exact cURL of the request + full response + expected vs actual
A screenshot of the test code
The link to the feature file
m8.why: With cURL + response the dev reproduces it in 30 seconds. Without it, the ticket bounces back with “can't reproduce”.

m8.q: Who consumes the report and what does each one need?
o: Dev: failure detail with evidence · Lead/PO: status per requirement · Manager: trend and risk — a navigable report serves all three
m8.why: A single-level report fails someone: it either drowns the manager in stack traces or leaves the dev without data. Navigability solves both.

m8b.q: Which of these INVALIDATES a sign-off?
o: An honest red documented as a known issue
An @IGNORE with an open ticket and an exit condition
m8b.why: Unresolved placeholders break the audit chain. An honest, documented red does NOT invalidate — a lie does.

m8b.q: Why is the certification signed by a human?
o: Because it involves risk judgment and professional accountability that can't be automated
Because the AI has no account in the test management tool
m8b.why: Signing means taking responsibility. Automating the signature is automating accountability — forbidden.

m8b.q: What does a useful certification Definition of Done contain?
o: Verifiable conditions: linked scenarios, recorded execution, attached evidence, declared known issues
m8b.why: A useful DoD is an auditable checklist, not a feeling. If it can't be verified, it isn't a DoD.

m8b.q: A user story has 2 scenarios excluded with @IGNORE (vendor bug, open ticket). Can the story be certified?
o: No: with open known issues the story stays open — you communicate the status, you don't sign a completeness that doesn't exist
Yes, if the @IGNORE is well documented
m8b.why: A well-done @IGNORE manages the RUN; closing the story requires what was excluded to be resolved. Signing with gaps is signing polite lies.

m8b.q: “I have the evidence on my machine; if someone asks I'll send it.” Is that valid for the sign-off?
o: Yes, as long as it exists
No: the evidence must be ATTACHED/published in the chain (ticket/test management tool/report) — what isn't recorded doesn't exist for the audit
Yes, if you back it up
It depends on the file size
m8b.why: The sign-off must outlive you: if you go on vacation (or leave the company), the full chain must be reconstructable without you.

m8b.q: Why does the method ask for a single-file report as evidence?
o: Self-contained: it gets attached to the ticket and opens anywhere years later, without depending on the report server still being alive
m8b.why: CI servers rotate and delete artifacts. A self-contained file attached to the ticket is evidence that doesn't expire.

m8b.q: Who defines the certification Definition of Done?
o: The team agrees on it ONCE and it applies equally to everyone — your personal checklist is your implementation of that agreement
m8b.why: One DoD per person = random standards per story. The team agreement is what makes it auditable and fair.

m8b.q: An audit 6 months later asks about story HU-482. What must be possible?
o: The QA who tested it explains it from memory
Rebuilding the full chain (requirement→cases→execution→evidence→closure) from the records, WITHOUT depending on anyone
m8b.why: Certifying means leaving a self-explanatory trail. If the answer to the audit is one person's memory, there was no certification.

m8b.q: What separates the dev's “done” from the method's “certified”?
o: Dev done = code integrated and working; certified = tested against its criteria WITH recorded evidence and traceability
m8b.why: Between “it works in the demo” and “I can prove what was tested and what wasn't” there's a chasm: that chasm is your job.

m8b.q: The deadline is looming and you're pressured to sign with 30% of the suite not run. The method's answer?
o: You don't sign false completeness: you present the real status (what was tested, what wasn't, risk of what's pending) and whoever decides takes the risk IN WRITING
Sign and run the rest later
m8b.why: Your signature says “this was tested”. The business can accept risk — it's their right — but documented and under their own name, not inside your signature.

m9.q: Which one is a well-placed quality gate?
o: The pipeline retries until it passes
The PR can't be merged if the critical suite fails
A coverage badge in the README
Running the tests after the deploy
m9.why: The gate blocks BEFORE the merge. After the deploy it's no longer a gate, it's an autopsy.

m9.q: A test fails 1 out of 10 runs with no code changes. What do you do?
o: Quarantine: it leaves the gate, a ticket to fix the root cause, and it is NOT deleted
Delete it: it's more trouble than it's worth
m9.why: A flaky test in the gate trains the team to ignore reds. Quarantine + root-cause fix; deleting it loses coverage.

o: Reproducible environment: same browser/Node versions locally and in CI — kills “it passes on my machine”
m9.why: Reproducibility is the point: if local and CI differ, every red opens a debate instead of a fix.

m9.q: What is sharding and what does it require?
o: Splitting the suite across N machines in parallel — it requires INDEPENDENT tests (no order or shared state)
m9.why: --shard=1/4 only works if any subset can run on its own. The isolation from module 5 is what makes sharding possible.

m9.q: The CI run finished. Where are the report and the trace for debugging?
o: They were lost with the runner
In the pipeline ARTIFACTS: the job uploads them (upload-artifact) and you download them from the run
You have to re-run to see them
m9.why: Runners are ephemeral. If the job doesn't publish the report/trace as an artifact, every CI failure is irreproducible by design.

m9.q: Your suite needs the staging API_KEY. Where does it live?
o: In the CI provider's SECRETS (encrypted, masked in logs) — never in the repo
m9.why: A secret in the repo is compromised from the first push (history never forgets). CI secrets exist exactly for this.

m9.q: “npm ci” takes 4 minutes on every run. What's the right optimization?
o: Dependency cache keyed to the lockfile: it's invalidated only when dependencies change
m9.why: A cache keyed by the lockfile hash gives you the best of both worlds: instant install when nothing changed, a clean one when something did.

m9.q: What runs on the PR, what on main and what in the nightly?
o: PR: smoke + critical suite (fast) · main: full suite · nightly: full regression + performance — fast feedback where it blocks
Only nightly, so as not to bother anyone
m9.why: The PR gate must be fast to be respected; the exhaustive stuff runs where it blocks no one. Each layer with its own time budget.

m9.q: Your gate takes 90 minutes and devs merge with “admin override”. What's the REAL problem?
o: A gate so slow it gets in the way stops being respected: it has to come down to minutes (sharding, risk-based selection) or it loses authority
m9.why: Friction always beats discipline. A control people route around controls nothing: the gate's speed IS part of its design.

m9.q: Why use the official Playwright Docker image (mcr.microsoft.com/playwright) with the SAME version as the npm package?
o: It's the only one that exists
It ships the exact browsers and system dependencies for that version — a mismatched image and package = weird browser failures
m9.why: Playwright pins browser versions per release. Image 1.44 with package 1.46 = cryptic crashes nobody links to the real cause.

m28.q: A workflow has the jobs lint and e2e, with no needs. lint fails. What happens to e2e?
o: It waits until you fix lint
It runs anyway, in parallel, because it doesn't depend on lint
m28.why: Without needs the jobs are independent. With needs: [lint], e2e would wait and be skipped when lint fails.

m28.q: The repo's npm cache is deleted. What should happen on the next run?
o: It fails because dependencies are missing
It takes longer and gives the same result
m28.why: The cache is a disposable optimization. If deleting it changes a result, that's a finding: something depended on it.

m28.q: The eval-gate check in qa-eval-lab comes out green in a repo without OPENAI_API_KEY. What does it tell you?
o: That the LLM approved every answer
That the UI tests passed and DeepEval and Promptfoo were skipped, as the ::notice says
That the key is misconfigured and the job failed silently
m28.why: Green is not the same as evaluated. You have to read which steps ran; the README states it under §Limits.

m28.q: Your check is green and required in your head, but main isn't protected. Someone opens a PR with red tests. What blocks the merge?
o: Nothing: without branch protection and a required check, the merge can still happen
GitHub blocks every PR with red checks by default
m28.why: A gate is two things: a required check and a protected branch. On 26-Oct-2026 none of the five repos in the real cases had main protected.

m28.q: A step says npm test || true. What changes?
o: It runs the tests in parallel
The step exits 0 even if the tests fail: the gate stops being a gate
m28.why: It's a hidden fail-open. You only see it if you read the log, which is why it's one of the week's mutations.

m28.q: Without the key, eval-gate prints a notice and comes out green. What kind of design is it and how do you make it fail-closed?
o: Fail-safe; it runs the full suite
Fail-open; you make it fail-closed by making the job fail (exit 1) when the secret is missing on the events where the gate must grade
m28.why: Fail-open: when in doubt, green. It's reasonable in a public repo without a key if it warns you, but it doesn't work as a merge gate.

m28.q: With retries: 2, a test fails and passes on the second attempt. What do you do?
o: You treat it as flaky: it stays flagged in the report, goes to quarantine with a ticket and isn't hidden
m28.why: Playwright reports it as flaky. In jev-ci-triage, “failed and passed on a retry in the same run” is flaky rule 1. A mutant runner uses retries: 0.

m28.q: What sets verify.yml apart from reproduce.yml in predictor-debugger?
o: verify.yml runs on every push and checks the fingerprint against stored verdicts; reproduce.yml is triggered by hand or by a v* tag, downloads data-v1 on a clean runner and recomputes
m28.why: A cheap pipeline for every change and an expensive one for the evidence. Both require the fingerprint with grep -q.

m28.q: Your check is green, but the branch has no protection and the check isn't required. What does it block?
o: Nothing: the merge can still happen
m28.why: The gate exists when the check is required on a protected branch.

m28.q: qa-eval-lab without OPENAI_API_KEY comes out green. What happened?
o: The LLM was evaluated and passed
The UI tests passed; the DeepEval and Promptfoo steps were skipped with a ::notice::
m28.why: Green is not evaluated: you have to read which steps ran.

m28.q: A step says npm test || true. What effect does it have?
o: The step goes green even if the tests fail
m28.why: It's a silent failure: the gate stops being a gate.

m28.q: How do a cache and an artifact differ?
o: The cache speeds things up and can disappear; the artifact is evidence to download and review
m28.why: Never store evidence only in the cache.

m28.q: Two jobs have no needs between them…
m28.why: needs creates the dependency; without it, each job starts on its own.

m28.q: Which gate order makes the most sense?
o: lint → typecheck → unit → API/contract → UI → performance → visual
m28.why: Cheap and fast first: if it fails, you don't spend minutes on the expensive stuff.

m28.q: In civica's ci.yml, why do the uploads have if: ${{ !cancelled() }}?
o: So nothing is uploaded if something fails
To upload the report and the ledger even if an earlier gate fails, unless the run is cancelled
m28.why: The most useful evidence is precisely the one from the run that failed.

m28.q: What does predictor-debugger's reproduce.yml do when you push a v* tag?
o: It downloads data-v1 on a clean runner, recomputes and requires the verdicts and the fingerprint with grep -q
m28.why: It's an evidence pipeline: the tag triggers the reproduction.

m28.q: restful-booker was red on October 15 and 16. Why?
o: npm run format:check (Prettier) found unformatted files
m28.why: A cheap, early gate caught the problem before the suites.

m27.q: A GitHub Actions job finishes on a hosted runner. What's left?
o: What you uploaded as an artifact, what you published in a release and what you committed
The whole runner disk, for 14 days
The npm cache with your reports
m27.why: The runner is discarded. Whatever didn't get out before is lost.

m27.q: You delete the cache and re-run. The result's fingerprint changes. What do you conclude?
o: It's normal, the cache changes everything
The cache needs to be refilled
It's a finding: the result depended on something that wasn't pinned
m27.why: The cache should only change the time. If the fingerprint changes, an input wasn't pinned.

m27.q: Why pin an image by digest (image@sha256:…) rather than by tag?
o: Docker doesn't accept tags in CI
A tag can be moved to another image; a digest names exactly the same content
m27.why: A pinned input is the precondition for repeating a run in another environment and getting the same fingerprint.

m27.q: The session drops and the global lock shows as free. Can you just relaunch the task?
o: Yes, a free lock proves the process died
No: in repro-ia-20261026 the free lock was judged «not sufficient alone to prove old driver absent» and nothing was relaunched while the old process's identity was uncertain
Only if the disk is full
m27.why: receipts/interruption.json says so. A process still alive in another namespace could write over your checkpoint.

m27.q: The 81 R1 files were regenerated and differ from the published ones by at most 8.9e-16. What are they?
o: A new run, declared as such: none is bit-for-bit identical, and the fingerprint and verdicts do match
m27.why: Regenerating is not recovering. The original arrays disappeared with the ephemeral executor; results_scope.txt states it as NEW RUN.

m27.q: Why write a checkpoint to a temporary file and then mv it?
o: So that, if the process dies halfway, there's no half-written checkpoint under the real name
m27.why: A rename is atomic on the same file system: either the full checkpoint is there or it isn't.

m27.q: When resuming, how do you know a task is already done?
o: Because its hash verifies against the stored receipt, and you check it with the lock held
m27.why: Existing isn't enough: the file may be truncated or stale. In the release, each task's SHA and rows are checked under lock.

m27.q: The release says «This is not an independent review». Why does it matter?
o: An AI assistant operated it under the author's direction; reproduced is not the same as reproduced by a third party
m27.why: A matching fingerprint is still strong evidence, but whoever produced it isn't independent. The next step is for another person to run reproduce.yml or the package.

m27.q: A GitHub Actions job finishes. What happens to the files it generated that you didn't upload?
o: They stay on the runner for the next job
m27.why: Every job starts clean and its disk dies with it.

m27.q: Why pin an image by digest and not by tag?
o: Tomorrow the tag may point to another image; the digest identifies exactly the same one
m27.why: A pinned input is the precondition for repeating a run.

m27.q: Release repro-ia-20261026: what happened to the 81 arrays from the previous run?
o: They disappeared with the ephemeral executor; R1 was regenerated as a new run
The durable hashes and statistics stored as receipts
m27.why: What leaves as a receipt outlives the container.

m27.q: The 81 regenerated files aren't bit-for-bit identical (max 8.9e-16). What about the fingerprints?
o: They match the originals, as do the verdicts
m27.why: Bit-identical is not the same as verdict-identical.

m27.q: What is a flock for in a resumable run?
o: So no two processes do the same task and you resume without duplicating work
m27.why: In the package, each task's SHA and rows are checked under lock.

m27.q: You lost the session with the process running R4 and don't know if it's still alive. What does the receipt's policy say?
o: Don't relaunch while the old process's identity is uncertain
m27.why: receipts/interruption.json: losing the session doesn't prove the old process stopped.

m27.q: Where do you check that something is reproducible?
o: In a clean environment, from scratch, like reproduce.yml's fresh runner
m27.why: The author's machine hides everything that isn't pinned.

m10.q: p95 = 180 ms and average = 90 ms. What does it mean?
o: 5% of requests take MORE than 180 ms: the average hides the tail
m10.why: Percentiles show the tail the average hides — and your most annoyed users live in the tail.

m10.q: You want to know if the app can handle 6 hours of normal traffic without degrading (memory leaks). Which test?
m10.why: Soak = load sustained over time: it reveals leaks and slow degradation that a short test never sees.

m10.q: The first request to a Lambda takes 3 s; the following ones, 120 ms. What is it?
o: Cold start — include it in the SLO or mitigate with warmers/provisioned concurrency
m10.why: It's serverless physics, not a bug. Your job is to decide whether the SLO tolerates it and to validate the mitigation.

m10.q: Where does the pass/fail criterion of a well-built k6 test live?
o: In the eye of whoever watches the dashboard
In the script's THRESHOLDS (p95<300ms, error_rate<1%): the test fails on its own, with no manual interpretation
m10.why: Without thresholds, a load test is an opinion. With thresholds it's a real test: automatable, gateable and beyond debate.

m10.q: Why ramp up the load GRADUALLY in a stress test?
o: So you don't scare the server
To find THE POINT where the system starts to degrade — if you hit it with everything at once, you know it dies but not when
m10.why: The value of stress testing is the curve: at what point latency rises, when errors appear. The ramp-up draws that curve.

m10.q: VUs go up: throughput plateaus but latency stays stable. What does it mean?
o: All good: latency is the only thing that matters
The system saturated a bottleneck (connection pool, CPU, workers): it processes the same amount even if you ask for more
You need more VUs to measure
m10.why: Flat throughput with growing demand = capacity limit found. Latency and throughput tell different stories: look at both.

m10.q: What's the difference between an SLI and an SLO?
o: SLI = the measured metric (actual p95) · SLO = the target on that metric (p95 < 300 ms 99% of the time)
The SLO is the legal version of the SLI
The SLI is for infra and the SLO for business
m10.why: First you define WHAT you measure (SLI), then HOW MUCH is acceptable (SLO). Your k6 thresholds are executable SLOs.

m10.q: You run the load test on a staging with half of prod's resources. What can you conclude?
o: Trends and relative REGRESSIONS (is this release slower than the previous one?) — not prod's absolute numbers, the infra differs
m10.why: A small staging works as a regression detector by comparing against itself. Extrapolating absolutes to prod without the same infra is fiction.

m10.q: As load rises, the error rate goes up but latency for the requests that DO respond holds steady. Most likely hypothesis?
o: A resource with a hard limit rejecting the excess (rate limit, full pool, saturated queue): it answers some quickly and drops the rest
m10.why: Fast rejection + stable success = something is dropping requests at the door. It's a different pattern from general degradation — and it's investigated differently.

m10.q: Why connect k6 to Grafana if k6 already prints the summary?
o: Correlated time series (latency vs errors vs VUs on the SAME time axis): the final summary doesn't show WHEN each thing happened
m10.why: “p95=800ms” doesn't say whether it was constant or a spike at minute 12 when the GC kicked in. The time series is what explains why.

m20.q: You change one word of the text the model judges and run in replay mode. What should happen?
o: It passes with the previous recording
The fixture is missing and the test is left unverified: it doesn't pass
The model is called live without warning
m20.why: The key is the hash of (model, redacted state, question): a different input never reuses an old response.

m20.q: Why is a recording's key a hash of the request and not the test name?
o: Because that way a change in the request invalidates the recording; with the test name an old response would be reused
m20.why: The test name doesn't change when you change the question; the hash does.

m20.q: An “ambiguous” verdict on a semantic assertion…
o: Is retried until it says yes
m20.why: playwright-jev, ADR 0001: anything ambiguous or unverified never passes.

m20.q: IMDb blocks bots and your real E2E can't run in CI. What does civica do?
o: A deterministic mock layer, and the real E2E skips with an honest reason
m20.why: A skip with a reason keeps the gap visible; deleting or retrying hides it.

m20.q: What does a CI that runs from recordings gain?
o: It's reproducible, needs no keys or network and gives the same answer on every run
m20.why: The same input gives the same verdict: what changes is your code, not the service's mood.

o: A short record of an architecture decision: context, decision and consequences
m20.why: It writes down why something was decided, so nobody undoes it without knowing.

m20.q: Your recording is six months old and the provider changed the model. What do you do?
o: I re-record on purpose (record mode) and review the verdict diff before accepting it
m20.why: Recording is a decision: the verdict diff is reviewed like any other change.

m20.q: What gets redacted before sending a state to an external model?
o: Tokens, emails, JWTs, cards and personal paths
m20.why: Whatever leaves your machine leaves redacted; jev-ci-triage does it in src/redact.ts.

m11.q: Why separate a “director” AI from an “executor” AI?
o: Planning with broad context and executing close to the code perform better than a single AI doing everything
m11.why: Planning and execution are different workloads: separating them performs better with any pair of tools.

m11.q: According to the delegation mental test, which task do you NOT delegate to the AI?
o: Generating steps from an OpenAPI contract
Deciding whether a contract mismatch blocks the release
Writing a mechanical POM on a clear convention
m11.why: Business/risk judgment + accountability = human. Mechanical work on a clear convention can be delegated.

o: That the AI is safe to use
That its mistakes arrive in a confident tone: ALWAYS review the diff, even if it sounds convincing
That it only fails on complex code
m11.why: Tone confidence doesn't correlate with correctness. The diff is always reviewed — no exceptions.

m11.q: What are the 5 blocks of a good prompt according to the method?
o: Context + Input + Instruction + Constraints + Expected output
m11.why: Each block removes a class of failure: without constraints it invents scope; without expected output, the format is a lottery.

o: Reusable recipes with <...> placeholders for the craft's repeated tasks — “from 10 minutes to 1”
m11.why: The task you do 20 times deserves a tested template with placeholders. A handcrafted prompt every time reinvents mistakes already solved.

m11.q: The AI generated a test against POST /users/validate… and that endpoint does NOT exist in the contract. What happened and what do you do?
o: The contract is out of date
Hallucination: it invented the endpoint with total confidence — the contract goes AS INPUT in the prompt and the diff is reviewed against it
You test it to see if it exists
m11.why: The AI fills gaps with plausibility, not truth. Real input (the contract) + review against the input = the antidote.

m11.q: What role does copilot-instructions.md (or Cursor's rules) play?
o: It's “the IDE's CLAUDE.md”: it connects the director AI's plan with the execution — the executor inherits conventions and constraints
m11.why: Without that artifact, the executor improvises its own style and the director's plan gets lost in translation.

m11.q: When should you NOT use AI for a QA task?
o: When you can't yet EVALUATE its output (you don't master the topic): you wouldn't tell the correct from the plausible
m11.why: That's why the module comes at the end of the course: AI amplifies those who know and confuses those who don't. Judgment first, then amplification.

m11.q: What does Playwright + MCP + AI (the cluster that dominates job openings) enable?
o: The AI can EXECUTE and inspect the real browser (run flows, read the DOM, verify) — not just write code blindly
m11.why: With MCP the AI goes from “writing tests that might work” to “actually testing and correcting itself” — that's why the market pays for it.

m11.q: You receive an AI-generated suite. What do you look for FIRST in the review?
o: Weak assertions (expect(true)), loose schemas and brittle selectors: the three typical vices the AI uses to “make tests pass”
m11.why: AI optimizes for “make it pass”, not “make it validate”. A green test that asserts nothing is worse than no test: it gives false confidence.

m14.q: You want your assistant to never push to main. Where does that rule live?
o: In the prompt: “please don't push to main”
In a hook that blocks the command with exit 2, plus branch protection on the repo
m14.why: A prompt is a request the model can overlook; a hook that exits with a non-zero code is a wall that can also be tested.

m14.q: You wrote the hook that blocks pushing to main. How do you know it works?
o: I tried it once and it blocked
I attack it with cases that try to slip through: chained commands, a bare git push while on main…
I ask the assistant whether it works
I trust it because the code is short
m14.why: WAR thread: the barrier is tested like the product. And attacking it pays off: a mutation found that git -c and git --no-pager slipped through, and commit 1b01c66 fixed it with new tests.

m14.q: The assistant tells you “I ran the suite and everything passed”. What do you sign?
o: I sign: the assistant is reliable
Nothing until I have a command, commit and exit code I can re-run
I sign if the answer sounds confident
I sign if it attaches a nice summary
m14.why: Evidence can be re-run: command + commit/hash + exit code. A sentence is not evidence.

m14.q: What goes in the repo's AGENTS.md (Codex) or CLAUDE.md (Claude Code)?
o: The project's API key, so the assistant doesn't ask for it
Frequent commands, conventions and what's forbidden
Nothing: the assistant already knows everything
m14.why: It's versioned project context. Secrets never go in committed files.

m14.q: The AI service that decides which tests to run isn't responding. What should happen?
o: Skip the doubtful tests to avoid delays
Mark the build green with a note
Retry with no limit until it responds
m14.why: Fail-safe: when in doubt, go conservative. jev-test-impact runs everything when the model fails.

m14.q: Your CI rebuilds the report from fixtures and compares it with the committed one. They differ. What does it mean?
o: Something changed (code, fixture or question) and the published report no longer matches: CI must fail
That the committed report must be deleted
m14.why: That's how agent-eval-jev works: the published evidence has to come from the current code, or CI turns red.

m14.q: The judge's recorded responses are stored with the exact hash of the request. What for?
o: So that a change in the question or the trace never reuses an old response
m14.why: If you change the question, the hash changes and the old recording no longer applies: reproducible replay with no stale responses.

m14.q: An assistant ran your full reproduction under your direction. How do you report it?
o: I say an assistant ran it under my direction and that it isn't an independent review
As if another person had done it
m14.why: predictor-debugger states it that way. What the reader needs to weigh the evidence gets said.

m14.q: Which part of the cycle do you NOT delegate to the assistant?
m14.why: The assistant designs, executes and audits; the person decides and signs. Certification is human.

m14.q: The assistant proposes loosening an assert because “the test fails over a detail”. What do you do?
o: I accept: it saw the error
I check against the contract: if the service breaks it, it gets reported and the assert stays
I mark it @IGNORE without a ticket
m14.why: The classic AI anti-pattern is adapting the test to the response. A false green is worse than an honest red.
